conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be walking you through a short screening tool called the EPDS, which looks at how moms are feeling in the weeks after birth. It’s simply a way to check in on your emotional well-being and see what extra support might be helpful right now. Everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days; each one is quick and conversational. Ready to start?

Over the last week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Hi Sarah. I... I can laugh sometimes, but it feels like I have to remind myself to do it, you know? Things that used to make me chuckle right away just don’t hit the same. I’d say I manage to laugh or joke maybe a couple of times in the day, but it’s definitely less than I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I mean, I can still laugh, but it feels kind of forced or distant—like I’m watching myself instead of really feeling it. Most of the week it’s just “meh,” maybe once or twice something actually felt funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to look forward to stuff—like when my mom offers to come hold the baby so I can take a walk—but even when I plan it, the excitement feels kind of flat. I still go, and parts are nice, but the happy “can’t-wait” feeling I used to get isn’t really there anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

I do catch myself doing that—like if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I’ll think “maybe I’m not doing something right” or “I should know better by now.” It’s not every hour or anything, but a few times this week I’ve felt that little pang of “this is my fault,” even when I know logically it probably isn’t.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… that happens. Sometimes I’ll just be sitting there, baby’s asleep and everything’s quiet, but my chest feels tight and my mind jumps to “what if his breathing sounds weird?” or “what if I’m missing something?” I know there’s no real reason, but the worry still bubbles up most days.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not exactly panicky—more like this sudden rush of “something’s wrong” that lasts a minute or two. It happened twice this week: once when I was washing bottles and once when I laid the baby down. My heart sped up and I felt kind of shaky, but I could talk myself down after a bit.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like that lately. I’ll be feeding him and notice the laundry pile or remember I still haven’t answered my friend’s text, and it’s like everything stacks up at once. I usually push through, but by dinnertime I’m just wiped and thinking “I can’t keep up with all this.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m so unhappy I can’t sleep—it’s more that my mind won’t settle. I’ll lie down exhausted, then start replaying every little thing I did that day, worrying I burped him wrong or didn’t sterilize the pacifier long enough. Takes me maybe an hour to drift off, and then I’m up with him every couple hours anyway.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I do feel that way some of the time—not all day, but it sneaks in. Like yesterday afternoon I was rocking the baby and suddenly felt this heaviness, kind of weepy for no clear reason. It passes, but it’s definitely happened a few evenings this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I haven’t cried a lot—just once this week. It was the night my husband found me folding onesies at midnight; I felt silly for being awake so late and the tears slipped out for maybe a minute. It wasn’t an all-out sob, just a quick spill-over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I get tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again and be okay for the baby.

It sounds as though you're working so hard to be the mum you want to be while feeling as if joy and energy have quietly slipped away. You described laughter feeling distant, excitement about small outings falling flat, and a heavy sense that everything is piling up beyond what you can manage. On top of that, worries pop up even when your baby is safe, and brief surges of panic catch you off-guard. You've noticed tears coming more often and a new habit of blaming yourself when your little one is unsettled, yet you clearly care deeply and want to feel like "you" again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter feels forced/distant and only occasionally funny, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes noticeably diminished anticipatory enjoyment that is "kind of flat" and missing the former "happy 'can't-wait' feeling," aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a few times this week" when baby is fussy, aligning with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries occurring "most days" without real cause, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden episodes of unexplained fear with physical symptoms (heart racing, shaky) that resolve quickly, fitting "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and difficulty keeping up, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeable sadness occurring "some of the time" on multiple evenings this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 16 places you above the 14-point cut-off indicating probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>, supported by diminished enjoyment (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), frequent low mood, self-blame, and daily anxiety. These map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>: depressed mood most days, markedly reduced interest/pleasure, fatigue-feeling overwhelmed, and associated anxiety. Items Q2, Q3, Q6, Q8 scored ≥2 confirm mood disturbance, while Q4 and Q5 highlight significant anxiety symptoms. Denial on Q10 lowers acute self-harm risk yet does not remove clinical urgency. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health team to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> tailored for postpartum depression/anxiety
3. Discuss with your doctor whether an <med>SSRI medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding might help
4. Plan daily 15-minute blocks of restorative activity (shower, short walk, quiet tea) while a trusted adult watches the baby
5. Reach out tonight to a support person or partner so you're not managing these feelings alone; share your EPDS result
6. Call 988 (US) or your local crisis line if distress escalates or you ever think of self-harm; help is available 24/7
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant age not specified)  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: [name], LCSW  

**Symptoms & Concerns Reported**  
- Anhedonia: diminished capacity to enjoy previously pleasurable activities; laughter described as “forced/distant”  
- Low mood: intermittent sadness, “meh” or weepy episodes several evenings per week  
- Guilt / self-blame: attributes infant fussiness to personal inadequacy (“I should know better”)  
- Anxiety: near-daily tension, “tight chest,” intrusive “what-if” worries even when baby is safe  
- Brief panic-like surges (2×/week) lasting ~1 min with autonomic arousal  
- Overwhelm / poor coping: reports “stacking up” chores, feels “wiped” by evening  
- Sleep-onset difficulty due to ruminative worry; not linked to infant schedule  
- Crying episode (1×/week) precipitated by sense of inadequacy  
- Denies any self-harm thoughts  

**Pattern Summary**  
Persistent low/flat mood, loss of enjoyment, cognitive self-criticism, daily anxiety with mild panic features, situational tearfulness, and subjective functional overload consistent with probable postpartum depression ± co-occurring anxiety disorder.  

**Screening Significance**  
Meets threshold items for further evaluation of postpartum depression (Q2, Q3, Q8, Q6) and postpartum anxiety (Q4, Q5). Denies suicidal ideation; no current safety concern identified.  

**Recommendation**  
Refer for comprehensive perinatal mental health assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and psychoeducation about PPD/PPA; consider supportive counseling and/or medication consult as indicated.
